opus-5.5.text:
Having access to a model like Gemini has really changed how I think about visual generalization. In the early days of robot learning, we trained policies largely from scratch. A robot would learn to pick up a red cup on a particular table under particular lighting, and if you moved it to a different kitchen or swapped the cup for a blue mug, performance would often collapse. We spent a huge amount of effort on domain randomization, data augmentation, and sim-to-real tricks just to get a bit of robustness to visual changes.

What a foundation model brings is that much of that visual understanding is already there. Gemini has seen an enormous variety of images and videos from the internet: different objects, scenes, lighting conditions, viewpoints. When we build a robot model on top of that, the robot doesn't need to learn from its own limited data what a mug is, or that a mug on a cluttered counter is the same kind of thing as a mug on a clean table. That knowledge transfers. We've seen that robots built this way handle new objects, new backgrounds, and new environments far better than anything we trained from robot data alone.

It has also shifted my view of where the bottleneck is. I used to think visual generalization was one of the hardest problems in robotics. Now I think it's largely, though not completely, addressed by these large pretrained models. The harder remaining problems are physical: dexterity, contact, force, and understanding how things actually move and deform when you interact with them. You can't learn much of that from watching internet videos, because the information about forces and tactile feedback simply isn't in pixels. So the robot data we collect now goes much further, because we're not wasting it on teaching the robot to see. We can focus it on teaching the robot to act.

There's one more piece I find exciting. Visual generalization and semantic generalization are tightly coupled. Because Gemini understands language and the world together, a robot can follow an instruction like "put the snack a kid would like into the bag," and it has to recognize the objects visually and reason about them. That combination of seeing and understanding is something we could barely imagine a few years ago, and it's a big reason I believe general-purpose robots are now within reach, even though there's still a lot of hard work ahead on the physical side.

r001.rationale: The candidate says foundation models changed its view: visual generalization once seemed among robotics’ hardest problems, but is now largely addressed.

r002.rationale: It credits Gemini’s exposure to diverse images and videos with transferring visual knowledge, but does not identify a vision encoder as the source.

r003.rationale: The candidate says pretrained models largely address visual generalization, but does not clearly state that they can provide it without further research specifically targeting it; it also qualifies that the problem is not completely addressed.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. I'd say it changed how I think about the problem at a pretty fundamental level.

Before we had access to something like Gemini, visual generalization in robotics was basically a data problem that we tried to solve from scratch. You'd collect robot demonstrations, train a policy, and then discover it fails the moment you change the lighting, move the camera a few centimeters, or put a slightly different mug on the table. So a huge amount of effort went into domain randomization, augmentation, sim-to-real tricks, all of it trying to manufacture visual robustness from a relatively small amount of robot data. And it never felt like we were getting at the root of the issue, because the robot had only ever seen a few thousand hours of the world.

What a strong foundation model gives you is a visual and semantic understanding that was learned from, essentially, the whole internet. The model already knows what a mug is, that it has a handle, that handles are for grasping, that a red mug and a blue mug are the same kind of object. So the question for robotics shifts. It's no longer "how do I teach the robot to see," it's "how do I connect this very rich understanding of the world to actual physical actions without destroying it." That's a very different research question, and honestly a more interesting one.

The second thing it shaped is my sense of where the real bottleneck is. Once perception and semantics are largely handled, you realize that what's missing is the embodied part: physical common sense, understanding of contact, forces, how objects behave when you push them, what happens over time when you act. Internet data is very thin on that. So the foundation model makes the gap very legible. It tells you exactly what you still have to collect from the physical world, and what you can inherit for free.

And the third thing, which I think people underestimate, is that it changes how you evaluate. When the model already generalizes semantically, you stop testing on "can it pick up the training object" and start testing on genuinely novel objects, novel instructions, novel environments. Your bar for what counts as generalization goes way up, because the capability is finally there to aim at it.

So in short, access to Gemini didn't just give us a better perception module. It reframed robot learning as the problem of grounding a model that already understands the world into a body that has to act in it, and I think that's the right framing for where the field is going.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts visual generalization as a difficult data problem requiring extensive robustness work with a foundation model that changes the research focus, showing a changed view of the problem’s difficulty.

r002.rationale: It attributes the model’s visual and semantic understanding to learning from the whole internet, but does not identify Gemini’s vision encoder or clearly attribute the generalization to that component’s exposure to diverse visual data.

r003.rationale: The response says the foundation model already provides visual and semantic understanding, so the robotics task shifts from teaching the robot to see toward grounding that understanding in physical action.

astra-6.text:
I think access to a strong foundation model like Gemini helps us separate two challenges: understanding what a robot sees and knowing how to act on it. A model might recognize an object in a new environment, understand an instruction, and connect that instruction to the scene. That gives us a powerful starting point for visual generalization.

But recognizing a cup doesn’t necessarily mean you can pick it up. The robot still has to understand the geometry, choose a grasp, and respond to what happens during contact. So the question becomes: how much of that broad visual understanding transfers into reliable physical behavior?

For me, the exciting possibility is that we don’t have to learn every visual concept from robot experience alone. We can build on the foundation model’s knowledge and use robot experience to ground that knowledge in action. But we still need to test carefully: does the robot succeed when the lighting changes, when the background changes, or when it encounters an object it hasn’t manipulated before? That’s where we find out whether visual understanding is actually helping the robot generalize.

r001.rationale: The response calls Gemini a “powerful starting point,” but does not state that access changes researchers’ perception of how difficult visual generalization is.

r002.rationale: It does not attribute visual generalization to the vision encoder’s prior exposure to diverse visual data.

r003.rationale: It says robot experience is needed to ground the model’s knowledge in action and calls for careful testing, rather than stating that the model can provide visual generalization without targeted research.

sol-6.1.text:
I think access to a strong foundation model like Gemini helps us separate two challenges. One is understanding what the robot is seeing: recognizing objects, interpreting a scene, and connecting that scene to a language instruction. The other is knowing how to act in that scene. A model can recognize a cup in an unfamiliar kitchen, but that doesn’t automatically mean a robot can grasp it reliably.

So it changes the question we ask about visual generalization. Instead of asking whether we can train perception for every new environment, we can ask how much of that understanding transfers from a foundation model, and what still needs to be learned through interaction. For robotics, the important test is whether that understanding leads to successful actions when the objects, lighting, or background change.

r001.rationale: The response says a foundation model changes which questions researchers ask, but does not state that it changes how difficult they perceive visual generalization to be.

r002.rationale: It does not attribute Gemini’s visual generalization to its vision encoder or to extensive exposure to diverse visual data.

r003.rationale: It says some understanding may transfer, while other capabilities still need learning through interaction; it does not say visual generalization requires no additional targeted research.
